    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763447/original/file-20261001-60-53vxfr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A case alleging that a Cornell sophomore was sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members is drawing national attention.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/students-walk-and-ride-across-the-campus-of-cornell-news-photo/2297900593?phrase=cornell%20university%20campus&amp;adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Universities have been trying for years to cut back on the abuses among fraternities, with limited resources and limited success.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/doe-cornell-new-york-supreme.pdf">new lawsuit</a>, filed by a former Cornell University student in September 2026, is now rattling higher education and <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/news/the-lede/how-the-cornell-seven-rape-case-became-a-national-scandal">drawing national attention</a>.</p>

<p>The person, identified as Jane Doe, has alleged that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and gang-raped her at an on-campus fraternity house when she was a sophomore in 2024.</p>

<p>Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to pursue criminal charges against the fraternity members in 2024. Following the filing of the case and emergence of new information, however, Van Houten <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/nyregion/van-houten-cornell-district-attorney.html">said on Sept. 26 that he is planning</a> “to discuss new evidence that exists” with the former Cornell student about her sexual assault claims. </p>

<p>The high-profile Cornell case is <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/wisconsin-fraternity-hazing-basement-rcna599852">just one of the latest</a> <a href="https://apnews.com/article/arizona-fraternity-pledge-hazing-death-b53c547d383082d33aebdb4950e0c550">fraternity scandals</a>. In August 2026, Pennsylvania announced <a href="https://www.psu.edu/news/campus-life/story/penn-state-responds-serious-criminal-charges-against-current-and-former-students">charges against current and former Penn State fraternity members</a> for their involvement in a criminal narcotics operation. </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://www.drsasso.com/">education scholar</a> who researches the experiences of undergraduate college students and fraternities, I believe that universities and colleges have not devoted enough resources toward <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/ijamh.2012.012">curtailing the hazing</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10778012211037381">sexual assault</a> and other kinds of dangerous behavior that sometimes happens at fraternities or other student organizations. </p>

<p>But there is only so much they can do – in part because beneath it all is a hypermasculine culture of proving one’s worth.</p>

<h2>A need for more enforcement</h2>

<p>In 1984, the National Minimum Drinking Age Act pressured states to set 21 as the minimum age to <a href="https://alcoholpolicy.niaaa.nih.gov/the-1984-national-minimum-drinking-age-act">purchase and consume alcohol</a>. All states made <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/23/158">21 the minimum age</a> by 1988. </p>

<p>The change meant that most college students could no longer legally purchase alcohol, leading some of them to drink in more private settings, like fraternity houses.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-04-28-mn-1607-story.html?">Some universities</a> felt concerned about the alcohol-related injuries and deaths occurring at fraternity houses. Schools also faced the possibility of <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/1990/524-pa-356-1.html?">lawsuits over underage</a> drinking.  </p>

<p>Harmful binge drinking remained a major problem on college campuses throughout the <a href="https://doi.org/10.15288/jsa.2002.63.136">1990s and early 2000s</a>. A lot of the documented hazing incidents <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9782661/">at fraternities during this time also involved alcohol</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ss.20249">Sexual assault on college campuses</a>, including at fraternities, was another major issue during this time.</p>

<p>A lot of universities started to respond to students’ excessive alcohol use, in part <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10410236.2023.2212447">through social norming</a>. This term means correcting people’s mistaken beliefs about what their peers normally do, like regularly drinking excessively. </p>

<p>They also tried other <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07448481.2021.1927048">harm-reduction strategies</a>, like sharing direct information with students about the negative effects of consuming alcohol, as well as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/hsc.13990">peer-led interventions</a> to try to reduce unsafe drinking or encourage alcohol moderation. </p>

<p>But they didn’t necessarily respond to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07448481.2021.2024210">related problems</a> surrounding hazing, such as substance misuse or addiction.</p>

<p>Some of the students’ parents, including those who had children who <a href="https://abcnews.com/GMA/News/parents-hazing-victims-react-house-passage-stop-campus/story?id=114075194">died as a result of hazing</a>, were concerned. They <a href="https://www.antihazingcoalition.org/about/">developed a large, nationwide parent lobby</a> to <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/parents-lobby-for-anti-hazing-bill/565684/">advocate for changes</a> in hazing laws across states. These groups, not the universities, have <a href="https://www.seattletimes.com/education-lab/biden-signs-anti-hazing-bill-backed-by-wa-parents/">been the most influential</a> in advocating for changes in hazing laws. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Groups of young people walk in front of buildings at dusk, with a dark blue sky." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763451/original/file-20261001-50-qrny79.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">While universities like Cornell can expel students for misconduct or crimes, they are limited in their response.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/students-walk-on-the-campus-of-cornell-university-on-news-photo/2297798094?phrase=cornell%20university%20campus&amp;adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Some prevention efforts</h2>

<p>It’s not that some universities haven’t tried to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ss.20528">reduce hazing on their campuses</a>. These efforts include practices such as hosting educational sessions, workshops, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ss.20524">speakers and even placing moratoriums</a> on social fraternity events that include alcohol. </p>

<p>Recent approaches have included teaching <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/csj.2016.0018">students how to recognize when their peers are emotionally distressed</a> and need help. </p>

<p>Some universities have started <a href="https://piazzacenter.psu.edu/who-we-are-piazza-history/">research centers on hazing</a> or hired full-time staff <a href="https://www.k-state.edu/student-support/conduct/hazing/">members whose jobs</a> <a href="https://www.health.columbia.edu/content/sexual-violence-response-staff-directory">involve prevention</a> and <a href="https://www.wm.edu/offices/wellness/ohp/violence-prevention/">response work</a> following a harmful incident such as hazing or sexual violence.</p>

<h2>Limited responses</h2>

<p>Universities can kick fraternities off campus and kick out athletes who are charged with <a href="https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/mqslr26&amp;div=32&amp;g_sent=1&amp;casa_token=&amp;collection=journals">hazing or sexual assault</a>. </p>

<p>But fraternities can also exist as private organizations, independent of a university. A university can withdraw recognition from a fraternity chapter and prohibit it from hosting events on campus, but that does not necessarily prevent the organization from <a href="https://myersedpress.presswarehouse.com/browse/book/9781975502645/Foundations-Research-and-Assessment-of-Fraternities-and-Sororities">hosting gatherings off campus</a>. </p>

<p>Another issue is that universities and colleges like Cornell have a civil process for dealing with hazing and other crimes, including sexual assault, but <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1079063217750864">not a criminal one</a>. Schools cannot <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0886260520925789">launch a criminal investigation</a>, but they can levy educational sanctions, including banning students from campus or taking away students’ scholarships. </p>

<p>Expelling students for illegal misconduct such as sexual assault and hazing is a really common approach, but that is about as far as these schools can go in terms of discipline.  </p>

<p>Schools may also cooperate with criminal investigations. Campus police, for example, can share their evidence and records with outside law enforcement. Or university staff may testify against students in court. But universities themselves cannot bring criminal charges. </p>

<p>After Jane Doe <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/doe-cornell-new-york-supreme.pdf">reported the incident</a> to university police, Cornell says it took action. </p>

<p>In a September 2026 statement, Cornell said its range of sanctions included “<a href="https://statements.cornell.edu/2026/20260928-da-investigation.cfm">expulsions and suspensions</a>.” A few students were asked to write essays, but Cornell says this wasn’t “as a sole consequence of their involvement.” </p>

<p>The Chi Phi chapter involved in the incident was also closed in 2024, according to Cornell. </p>

<p>Following the lawsuit and recent national attention it received, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/cornell-rape-allegations-investigation-7073e8da8b027fe9ee4530ea8a549f64">Cornell agreed to bring in</a> outside lawyers to determine whether it properly conducted the 2024 rape investigation. </p>

<h2>The role of masculinity</h2>

<p>Proving your masculinity <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/19496591.2019.1669455">can become a central part of proving your worth</a> and <a href="https://journal.libraries.wm.edu/jsflrp/article/view/730">fit at a fraternity</a>.</p>

<p>This <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10810730.2023.2222077">hypermasculine culture</a> – combined with a culture of secrecy – could be a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1097184X221133122">powder keg for sexual violence</a>. It’s a dynamic also seen <a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.focus.20170024">in the military</a> and on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/08862605231178356">sports teams</a>.</p>

<p>Hypermasculinity is not simply tied up in an individual’s behavior, but can become embedded within organizational cultures that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/19496591.2019.1669455">reward toughness, dominance, risk-taking and silence</a>. </p>

<p>In fraternities, these expectations may shape how members understand belonging and status. These issues may <a href="https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/men0000375">also discourage students</a> from <a href="https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/men0000180">expressing vulnerability</a> and seeking help. </p>

<p>Understanding these gendered and cultural dynamics is, I believe, essential to developing prevention efforts that address not only individual conduct, but also the organizational norms that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/csd.2016.0079">allow harmful behaviors to persist</a>.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293305/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>US regulators want to make corporate earnings reports less frequent, but investors have doubts</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763465/original/file-20261001-50-ym9m1p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8502%2C5668&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A new financial reporting proposal, pitched by Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins, has generated enormous opposition, from ordinary savers to industry groups.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=securities%20and%20exchange%20commission&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The U.S. government has pitched an obscure accounting rule change that has ignited <a href="https://www.wsj.com/finance/regulation/sec-quarterly-earnings-reports-complaints-2979d5a0">a firestorm</a> of opposition. If enacted, its effects might be felt from the capital markets to your retirement savings account.</p>

<p>At issue is <a href="https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026-42-sec-proposes-amendments-permit-optional-semiannual-reporting-public-companies">a proposal</a> by the <a href="https://www.sec.gov/">Securities and Exchange Commission</a> that would scrap a long-standing requirement for registered companies to disclose their earnings every three months. Instead, they would have the option to do so only every six months.</p>

<p>The agency says its <a href="https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/atkins-statement-proposing-release-semiannual-reporting-050526">proposal has two goals</a>: One is to reduce a company’s compliance costs needed to prepare financial statements; the other is to promote longer-term planning rather than a short-term fixation on earnings. A final decision is expected by late 2026.</p>

<p>These ideas may sound in the weeds to the average American, but the proposal has prompted opposition that is literally record-breaking ever since it was released for comments in May 2026. To date, <a href="https://tax.thomsonreuters.com/news/sec-faces-delays-on-semiannual-reporting-proposal-amid-record-number-of-comment-letters/">over 280,000 letters</a> have come in, with the vast majority against. By comparison, <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6717658">one study</a> that covered 417 different proposals over 30 years tallied more than 65,000 letters total.</p>

<p>I’m an accounting professor who has constructed <a href="https://tzachizach.github.io/sec-semi-annual-proposal-tracker/index.html">a tracker</a> that lets people scour the SEC docket and decipher the general sentiment of these comments. I found that the main driver of this hostility is concern that less frequent reporting would make it harder for investors to monitor companies’ performance and decision-making, because key information is withheld for longer periods. </p>

<p>This reduction in transparency carries another risk as well: It would likely make it more expensive for companies to raise capital. Once external monitoring is reduced, investors may demand a <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/248475">higher rate of return</a> because they have less information about the company’s health. That means the company would need to pay more for that uncertainty, whether through selling shares, borrowing from lenders or issuing bonds. </p>

<p>In short, there’s a trade-off between the cost of capital and transparency.</p>

<h2>A tsunami of opposition</h2>

<p>If a business wants to be a publicly traded company, it has to register with the SEC, which governs and regulates this process. Once registered, the company has to disclose its financial performance every three months, <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/07/2026-09095/semiannual-reporting">a requirement that has held since 1970</a>. </p>

<p>Whenever the agency issues a new rule, it opens it up to comments first, just like other government agencies do. That feedback is meant to shape the final rule before it becomes codified.</p>

<p>What’s unusual in this case is the overwhelming degree of opposition – more than 99% of all comments, many from retail and individual investors, according to my tracker.</p>

<p>“My husband worked for Enron. We lost most of our retirement savings when their fraudulent activity came to light,” <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-2576452.htm">wrote one commenter</a>. “We were still young enough to make some of that income back, but we knew many retirees who ended up working into their 80’s. Quarterly reporting is a gate keeper. Keep it.” </p>

<p><a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-2588027.htm">Wrote another</a>: “I rely on quarterly reporting for the same reason your child gets a quarterly report card. … There the metaphor ends, because a good teacher can catch failing performance and course correct with parents long before report cards are issued. Investors do not have that luxury.”</p>

<p>Some point out that the commission’s claim of company savings on compliance costs is overblown. The estimated average savings, according to the proposal, is <a href="https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11414.pdf">around US$200,000</a> a year per firm, which is a drop in the bucket for a typical public corporation. </p>

<p>But more broadly, the comments reveal how much this rule could matter to ordinary investors. Retirement savings, through accounts like 401(k) plans and individual retirement accounts, are directly exposed to company performance, whether or not the fund in question is diversified. That means any reduction in financial transparency has direct implications on how the investments of the funds are monitored. </p>

<p>That risk was laid out <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-944260-2915237.pdf">in a letter</a> from the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, or SIFMA. The trade group wrote that the estimated net savings “could be offset or outweighed by an increase in the cost of capital as investors demand higher risk premia for less timely information.”</p>

<p>Federated Hermes, an asset manager, <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-947359-2921191.pdf">also pointed</a> to this scenario: “Issuers that elect semiannual reporting may face signaling risks, as investors could interpret such a choice as reflecting reduced transparency,” the letter said. “This may affect analyst coverage and cost of capital.”</p>

<h2>Companies weigh in</h2>

<p>As for the companies themselves, it’s too early to say whether they would take advantage of the six-month option. But several have said they would choose to report less frequently. </p>

<p>For its part, the commission is still evaluating all the feedback before its leadership takes a vote. Traditionally, it’s led by five commissioners, with three representing the party in power and two from the opposition. However, in this case, the two Democratic seats in the minority are currently vacant, and one Republican seat is about <a href="https://www.plansponsor.com/hester-peirce-to-depart-as-sec-commissioner-on-october-2/">to be vacated</a>.</p>

On Sept. 30, 2026, it suggested a <a href="https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/2026/34-106537.pdf">rule change</a> so that the two votes would suffice.</p>

If enacted, its effects might be felt from the capital markets to your retirement savings account
At issue is a proposal by the Securities and Exchange Commission that would scrap a long-standing requirement for registered companies to disclose their earnings every three months
Instead, they would have the option to do so only every six months

The agency says its proposal has two goals : One is to reduce a company’s compliance costs needed to prepare financial statements; the other is to promote longer-term planning rather than a short-term fixation on earnings
A final decision is expected by late 2026

To date, over 280,000 letters have come in, with the vast majority against
By comparison, one study that covered 417 different proposals over 30 years tallied more than 65,000 letters total

Once external monitoring is reduced, investors may demand a higher rate of return because they have less information about the company’s health
That means the company would need to pay more for that uncertainty, whether through selling shares, borrowing from lenders or issuing bonds

If investors have less information about a company’s financial health, the uncertainty could make it more expensive for the company to raise capital

<title>White nationalism’s appeal runs deeper than partisan politics</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763218/original/file-20260930-50-ngmeha.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Members of Patriot Front hold flags on the National Mall in Washington on Jan. 23, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/March%20for%20Life/ab0ece7c18374f9eaab1819129664a0b/photo">AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As Americans prepared to celebrate the nation’s 250th birthday on the morning of July 4, sobering images flashed across their phones and TV screens. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/04/us/white-nationalists-march-in-washington-amid-250th-anniversary-celebrations.html">Hundreds of masked men marched</a> the streets of Washington carrying flags and chanting “Reclaim America!” It soon became clear from the logos on their identical baseball caps that the marchers were members of <a href="https://extremism.gwu.edu/patriot-front">Patriot Front</a>, a white nationalist group.</p>

<p>The march ended without incident. Still, it joined the 2017 “Unite the Right” <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/13/us/charlottesville-protests-unite-the-right.html">rally in Charlottesville</a>, Virginia, and the Jan. 6, 2021, <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/january-6-us-capitol-attack-128973">attack on the U.S. Capitol</a> – both of which culminated in deadly violence – as recent mass demonstrations with participants who openly embrace white nationalism. Members of a loosely organized movement that usually operates out of public view, white nationalists hold that shifting demographics <a href="https://www.economist.com/the-economist-explains/2019/08/14/what-is-white-nationalism">pose an existential threat</a> to the white race, which they view as culturally superior and deserving of power over other groups in the U.S.</p>

<p>Combined with the spread of white nationalist ideology from <a href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1536504218766547">obscure corners of the internet</a> into <a href="https://x.com/mattgaetz/status/1441807874053885952">mainstream politics</a>, these events have led many Americans to wonder: How extensive is white nationalism’s appeal among the broader public, and who is drawn to this extremist ideology?</p>

<p>We are political scientists who study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=RRG8_oAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">political behavior</a>, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=n2ZWYqoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">identity</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=fc0VgPAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">social media</a>. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11018-0">recently published research</a> in the scientific journal Nature, we offer some answers to these questions using national surveys we conducted with nearly 8,000 non-Hispanic white Americans from 2021 to 2025. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A crowd of men, some in helmets and protective gear, march with Confederate flags and other banners." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763442/original/file-20261001-50-lidaqb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">White nationalist demonstrators walk into Lee Park in Charlottesville, Va., on Aug. 12, 2017.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Unite%20the%20Right%20Rally-Trial/d1fad87e70d04855a4044ff4d4595bcb/photo">AP Photo/Steve Helber</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Asking Americans about white nationalism</h2>

<p>We expected many Americans would be unfamiliar with the term “white nationalism,” so we defined it for survey respondents with a brief statement covering the movement’s major tenets: the purported need to maintain a white majority in the U.S., claims about the superiority of white culture, and calls for white people to hold more political and economic power than other groups. We measured endorsement of the movement’s ideology, not participation in the movement itself or approval of its tactics.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11018-0/figures/1">We randomly varied</a> whether respondents saw the description before or after we asked whether they supported the white nationalist movement. Overall, nearly 5% of white adults – about 1 in 20 – said they did.</p>

<p>Those asked the question before seeing the description were less likely to express support at first, but their reported support rose after they read it. Along with several tests for possible response bias, this suggests that 5% is a reasonable lower-bound estimate of the true level of support. </p>

<p>Whether 1 in 20 white adults is a high or low number is a matter of interpretation. For context, it’s roughly the same as the share of American adults who identify as <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/510038/identify-vegetarian-vegan.aspx">vegetarian or vegan</a>. </p>

<h2>Young white men</h2>

<p>A number that jumped out to us was the share of white men under age 30 who support white nationalism: just over 13%, or <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02648-5">about 1 in 7</a>. This was more than twice the level of support for white nationalism among women in this age group: 6%. <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11018-0/figures/4">Endorsement of white nationalism among men significantly declined by age</a>: Only 2% of white men age 65 and over registered support. </p>

<p>Our discovery that white men born before the passage of the Civil Rights Act were more likely to reject white nationalism than those coming of age today may come as a surprise, as younger white Americans typically <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/707490">hold more tolerant views</a> on racial matters than their elders. But young men have long been <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/healing-from-hate/hardcover">overrepresented in extremist groups</a>, and white nationalism’s grievance narrative may resonate for young white men today as they <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/books/of-boys-and-men/">fall behind previous generations of men</a> on key indicators like finishing college, starting careers and forming families, as well as on their overall health.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Men in white face masks and dark shirts stand at a railing above a subway escalator with American flags behind them as a man rides the escalator below" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5678%2C3781&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763215/original/file-20260930-60-pp3ftn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Members of the white supremacist group Patriot Front gather in Washington on July 4, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/members-of-the-white-supremacist-group-patriot-front-gather-news-photo/2284619752">Finn Gomez/Getty Images News via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Online life</h2>

<p>Another key predictor of support: online social life that crowds out offline relationships. <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11018-0/figures/3">We asked respondents</a> to call to mind their three best friends and then to tell us whether each friend was known only offline, only online or both. </p>

<p>We found that the more best friends known only online, the stronger one’s support for white nationalism. The internet and particularly social media are channels through which people may be exposed to white nationalist content. They are also places where alienated people may turn for the human connections they lack offline. </p>

<p>Interestingly, we did not find a general relationship between more social media use and more support for white nationalism. So while online life appears to be related to support for white nationalism, what matters in our findings is not how much people use social media, but whether their closest friends are known only online.</p>

<h2>Individual and social strain</h2>

<p>Strain, whether defined as undergoing personal difficulties or being exposed to wider social distress, <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11018-0/figures/3">is also a strong predictor</a> of support for white nationalism. We asked respondents whether they had suffered from specific hardships over the past year, including the death of a loved one, losing a job, being the victim of a crime or getting divorced. Respondents experiencing more of these adversities were more likely to endorse white nationalism. </p>

<p>Social strain in the counties where respondents live – such as poverty, unemployment and population loss – emerged as another strong predictor of support for white nationalism, as did countywide rates of “deaths of despair,” which include <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691190785/deaths-of-despair-and-the-future-of-capitalism">suicide and deaths</a> associated with drug and alcohol use. In other words, support for white nationalism was higher among people living in more distressed or economically depressed places. </p>

<h2>More than just partisan politics</h2>

<p>White nationalism is <a href="https://www.amacad.org/publication/daedalus/bipartisan-origins-white-nationalism">often cast as a political phenomenon</a> by advocates, commentators and scholars, and indeed it is. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11018-0/figures/2">We found in our research</a> that white Democrats and liberals are significantly less likely to endorse white nationalism than white Republicans and conservatives. However, we also found high levels of support among those who were unsure of their ideology or partisanship, suggesting a potential untapped reservoir of political support for white nationalist ideas.</p>

<p>Still, our findings show that support for white nationalism cannot be explained solely by partisan politics. Larger forces, including generational change, the ubiquity of the internet and the <a href="https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-economics-080315-015041">strain Americans are experiencing in part due to profound economic transformation</a> are at work. </p>

<p>In our view, those who seek to understand and address this critical development in American public life must reckon with the broad structural shifts that have reshaped Americans’ identities, social relations and sense of economic security and that undergird white nationalism’s appeal to the broader public.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292676/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763428/original/file-20261001-50-8ji91u.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C787%2C4745%2C3163&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">In the fall of 1973, North Dakota&#39;s Drake school district burned 32 copies of Kurt Vonnegut’s &#39;Slaughterhouse-Five&#39; in a school furnace.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/open-book-is-on-fire-pages-are-engulfed-in-flames-royalty-free-image/1366290451?phrase=books%20burned%20in%20furnace&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Kristina Kokhanova/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Bruce Severy, a full-bearded, idealistic 26-year-old, moved from Southern California in 1973 to the small town of Drake, North Dakota, where he had accepted a job teaching English at the public high school. He, his small family and their menagerie of pets settled into a large, white frame house across from the school.</p>

<p>Severy’s progressive bent showed in the curriculum he taught. Insisting that his students should learn “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1973/11/16/archives/dakota-town-dumfounded-at-criticism-of-book-burning-by-order-of-the.html">how to think, not what to think</a>,” he assigned his sophomore literature class contemporary fiction to read, including Kurt Vonnegut’s “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/184345/slaughterhouse-five-by-kurt-vonnegut/">Slaughterhouse-Five</a>,” a strange and quirky anti-war novel published four years prior.</p>

<p>While Severy chose works that he believed could help his students make sense of the problems confronting society, they clashed with the conservative values of his new home. A parent eventually complained about profanity in “Slaughterhouse-Five.” In November 1976, the Drake school board voted unanimously to remove the book from school premises. School officials told students to turn in their copies, and their lockers were searched if they refused. The district went on <a href="https://www.inforum.com/newsmd/resentment-still-smolders-over-1973-book-burning-in-north-dakota">to burn 32 copies of the novel in the school furnace</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ODcyH4YAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">As a Vonnegut scholar</a>, I’m fascinated by the backlash to “Slaughterhouse-Five,” which is now widely taught in high schools and colleges across the country. Even though the U.S. Supreme Court eventually weighed in on Vonnegut’s novel, there are direct parallels between that controversy and the politics of school censorship cases today, which continue to target “Slaughterhouse-Five,” among countless other works.</p>

<h2>Vonnegut responds</h2>

<p>News of what happened in Drake spread quickly in the press. Those who objected to the school board’s actions made comparisons <a href="https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/book-burning">to Nazi book burnings</a>. The school district’s cause wasn’t helped by the fact that the superintendent’s last name was Fuhrman – evoking Adolf Hitler’s <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Fuhrer">formal title, Führer</a> – and the school board chairman’s last name was McCarthy, reminding the public of <a href="https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/censure/133Joseph_McCarthy.htm">Joseph McCarthy</a>, the disgraced anti-communist senator who sought to purge and censor Americans from all walks of life.</p>

<p>When Kurt Vonnegut learned of the case, he was both angry and saddened.  </p>

<p><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1982/02/07/opinion/books-into-ashes.html">In a letter</a> to the Drake school board, he insisted his books were “not sexy” and did not argue “in favor of wildness of any kind.” Instead, “they beg that people be kinder and more responsible than they often are.” He informed the board that <a href="https://indianahistory.org/blog/kurt-vonnegut-jr-indianapolis-and-slaughterhouse-five/">he was a decorated World War II veteran</a> who had fought against nations that hate books and burn them. He never received a reply.</p>

<p>The North Dakota incident, while the most egregious attempt to censor Vonnegut, was not the only case of its kind.  </p>

<p>As “Slaughterhouse-Five” made its way into high school and college curricula, it faced a backlash by parents and school boards who argued the novel was obscene and immoral. Its irreverent treatment of Christianity was deemed blasphemous, while its unsparing portrayal of the U.S. military’s bombing of Dresden, Germany, was condemned as anti-American.</p>

<p>The book has been challenged as recently as January 2026, when the ACLU filed a lawsuit on behalf of Vonnegut’s estate after Utah’s “<a href="https://olag.utleg.gov/olag-doc/2025-11_RPT.pdf">sensitive materials law</a>” gave school districts a mechanism to <a href="https://www.acluutah.org/press-releases/vonnegut-v-utah/">ban the novel</a>.</p>

<h2>The Supreme Court weighs in</h2>

<p>Censorship cases involving “Slaughterhouse-Five” are complex because they have occurred almost entirely in high schools rather than colleges. Schools must balance their responsibility to decide what material is appropriate for younger students with students’ First Amendment rights to receive information and ideas.</p>

<p>One important case dealing with these issues made it all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.</p>

<p>In 1976, several board members from the Island Trees School district in Long Island, New York, reacting to a list of “inappropriate” titles publicized by a conservative activist group, <a href="https://billofrightsinstitute.org/e-lessons/island-trees-school-district-v-pico-1982/">objected to 11 books</a> held in the districts’ school libraries or included in the curriculum.</p>

<p>Seven of the books were written by authors from minority ethnic or religious groups, including titles as seemingly inoffensive as “<a href="https://www.abebooks.com/best-short-stories-Negro-writers-anthology/31506162071/bd">Best Stories of Negro Writers</a>,” edited by <a href="https://theconversation.com/langston-hughes-domestic-pariah-international-superstar-133027">Langston Hughes</a>, and the young adult novel “<a href="https://archive.org/details/heroaintnothinbu00chil/page/n9/mode/2up">A Hero Ain’t Nothing but a Sandwich</a>” by Alice Childress.</p>

<p>The 11th book on the list was “Slaughterhouse-Five.” At a press conference, school board member <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1982/05/10/book-banning-spreads/8f892694-9de3-4faa-8d20-f168dd0ff7dc/">Frank Martin</a> read excerpts from the novel out loud, focusing on a passage where one of Vonnegut’s characters, <a href="https://blogs.charleston.edu/vonnegut/kilgore-trouts-works/">Kilgore Trout</a>, reimagines the story of Christ’s crucifixion. Trout claims that this revised story actually offered a better moral than the original Gospel story: It teaches people to be kind to everyone, not just the well connected. </p>

<p>Martin, however, declared that even if the rest of the book told the best story in the world, he wouldn’t want it in the school library “<a href="https://hechingerreport.org/the-magic-pebble-and-a-lazy-bull-the-book-ban-movement-has-a-long-timeline/">with this stuff in it</a>.”</p>

<p>Five high school students, led by 17-year-old Steven Pico, soon filed a lawsuit against the district, claiming the book removal was unconstitutional and that their First Amendment rights to freely receive information had been violated. The case wended its way through the lower courts for years, before it came to the Supreme Court in 1982.  </p>

<p><a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/457/853/">Board of Education v. Pico</a> was a tangled case. The justices wrote seven separate opinions and did not definitively settle the First Amendment issues. But a 5-4 majority did determine in favor of the students who argued that their case should have received a full trial rather than a summary judgment years ago.</p>

<p>As the only Supreme Court case to date involving censorship in school libraries, Pico, while a limited ruling, did set out general guidelines still used today.</p>

<p>The decision affirmed that school districts have the authority to supervise the education of students in their care and may remove materials that are, in the words of Justice William Brennan, “<a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1981/80-2043">pervasively vulgar</a>” or educationally unsuitable.  </p>

<p>But such a decision may not be based on a school district’s objections to the ideas expressed in the books. Books may not be removed on narrowly partisan or political grounds, and removal must comply with the “<a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1981/80-2043">transcendent imperatives of the First Amendment</a>.”  </p>

<h2>Book banning today</h2>

<p>Despite the fact that the justices ruled that books cannot be banned on partisan or political grounds, book banning has been on the rise in America since 2020. </p>

<p>The literary and free speech advocacy group <a href="https://pen.org/book-bans/">PEN America</a> documented 2,532 instances of book bans in public schools in 2021–22. That figure rose to 3,362 in 2022–23 and nearly tripled to 10,046 in 2023–24. </p>

<p>Since then, the numbers have dipped somewhat but are still alarmingly high.</p>

<p>Surprisingly, many of the school censorship cases today still focus on the same old issues affecting “Slaughterhouse-Five” over 50 years ago – profanity, sexual content and violence. John Green’s “<a href="https://www.marshall.edu/library/bannedbooks/looking-for-alaska/">Looking for Alaska</a>” has been the most frequently banned book in schools since 2021, mostly because of a brief, awkward sexual encounter between two main characters. </p>

<p>But fiction and memoirs focusing on gender identity and LGBTQ+ issues have increasingly become targets of censorship, abetted by right-wing parental rights groups like <a href="https://www.momsforliberty.org/">Moms for Liberty</a>. George M. Johnson’s memoir “<a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250895561/allboysarentblue/">All Boys Aren’t Blue</a>” and Maia Kobabe’s autobiographical graphic novel “<a href="https://www.marshall.edu/library/bannedbooks/gender-queer/">Gender Queer</a>” are among the most banned books in schools in recent years.</p>

<p>And like the majority of the books banned in the Pico case, books by Black authors remain high on the list of school censorship cases. Nobel Prize-winning author Toni Morrison’s first novel, “The Bluest Eye,” appears among the <a href="https://pen.org/top-52-banned-books-since-2021/">top 10 banned books</a> since 2021, and her Pulitzer Prize-winning “<a href="https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/toni-morrison">Beloved</a>” comes in at No. 26. Ironically, “Beloved” was also named the single best work of American fiction since 1980 <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20060806081907/https:/www.nytimes.com/2006/05/21/books/fiction-25-years.html?ex=1305864000&amp;en=d3f9cc78ce4c00b7&amp;ei=5088&amp;partner=rssnyt&amp;emc=rss">in a 2006 poll of writers and literary critics</a>.</p>

<p>Kurt Vonnegut believed in and argued for First Amendment rights his whole career. In 1976 <a href="https://soundcloud.com/conncollege/the-noodle-factory-by-kurt-vonnegut">he told students at Connecticut College</a> that language and literature were “holy” to him. He thought schools should make a point of exposing children to all sorts of opinions and information to make them better citizens. </p>

<p>But he wasn’t too hopeful. Arguing against book banning, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1976/03/28/archives/long-island-weekly-banned-authors-answer-back-they-see-the-move-as.html">he wearily concluded</a>, was like “attempting to explain America at its bravest and most optimistic to orangutans.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292561/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>How Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is helping kids start reading when they’re very young</title>
    <content type="html"><p>By the time <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/arts/music/dolly-parton-dead.html">Dolly Parton died on Aug. 25, 2026</a>, her <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/">Imagination Library</a> had gifted more than 332 million children’s books to babies and kids in all 50 states and <a href="https://theconversation.com/dolly-partons-imagination-library-what-its-success-means-for-childrens-reading-290977">four other countries</a>: Canada, the U.K., Australia and Ireland.</p>

<p>If they were set end to end, these books would circle the earth 1.8 times.</p>

<p>This free program mails an age-appropriate book monthly to each enrolled child from birth to age 5, meaning up to 60 books will fill these children’s shelves by the time they graduate from the program. </p>

<p>Though a selection committee tweaks the lists annually, each participant receives Watty Piper’s “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/series/DQR/the-little-engine-that-could/">The Little Engine That Could</a>” as their first book and Nancy Carlson’s “<a href="https://nancycarlson.com/look-out-kindergarten-here-i-come/">Look Out Kindergarten, Here I Come!</a>” as their last.</p>

<p>I’m an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Fe9cMqwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">information science professor who studies reading behavior</a>. In my research for an upcoming academic article about the Imagination Library, I’ve found that its free monthly books help families develop children’s literacy, prepare children for kindergarten and encourage a lifelong love of reading.</p>

<h2>Emphasis on early literacy</h2>

<p>Parton, most remembered as a popular country singer, embraced <a href="https://rockhall.com/inductees/dolly-parton/">many musical genres</a> during her long and successful career in show business. She was also a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/nx-s1-5945081/dolly-parton-podcast">songwriter, entrepreneur, actor and philanthropist</a>.</p>

<p>She created this program because she, like most early childhood literacy experts, believed that reading <a href="https://naeducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/Anderson-Hiebert-Scott-Wilkinson-Becoming-a-Nation-of-Readers.pdf">begins in the home</a>. That is, parents and other guardians are a child’s first teachers, and reading aloud to children <a href="https://naeducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/Anderson-Hiebert-Scott-Wilkinson-Becoming-a-Nation-of-Readers.pdf">contributes to their future literacy</a>.</p>

<p>First graders who struggle with reading usually <a href="https://people.uncw.edu/kozloffm/learningtreadandwrite.pdf">continue to have trouble with literacy later on</a>.</p>

<p>Very young children in lower-income households generally <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0042085916654525">have less access to books</a> and hear <a href="https://products.brookespublishing.com/Meaningful-Differences-in-the-Everyday-Experience-of-Young-American-Children-P14.aspx">fewer words</a> than higher-income kids. This class-based difference may lead to <a href="https://products.brookespublishing.com/Meaningful-Differences-in-the-Everyday-Experience-of-Young-American-Children-P14.aspx">disparities in reading skills later on</a>.</p>

<h2>A homegrown program</h2>

<p>Like Parton, who was born in a <a href="https://www.visitmysmokies.com/blog/dolly-parton/dolly-partons-childhood-home/">one-bedroom cabin in an Appalachian region</a> of Tennessee that had neither running water nor electricity, the Imagination Library’s origins were modest. It started in her hometown, hardscrabble Sevier County, in late 1995. Its initial order of 1,760 books was destined for the children who lived where she grew up.</p>

<p>The program came from “a very serious place in my heart,” <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2016/06/02/dolly-parton-how-my-father-inspired-the-imagination-library.html">Parton once said</a>. On many occasions, she emphasized how her own father’s illiteracy inspired her to found it – with him.</p>

<p>“Daddy couldn’t read nor write, and it always just seemed to cripple him, and he was embarrassed about it,” <a href="https://americanlibrariesmagazine.org/2018/01/02/newsmaker-dolly-parton/">Parton told American Libraries in 2018</a>. “My daddy just loved it when all the little kids would call me ‘The Book Lady,’” <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/books/dolly-parton-imagination-library.html">she said later</a>.</p>

<p>In contrast, Parton <a href="https://archive.org/details/dollymylifeother00part">was a bookworm</a>. “I always loved books,” she <a href="https://www.chicagoreviewpress.com/dolly-on-dolly-products-9781641600040.php">explained in an interview</a>. “I don’t remember learning to read, it was just something I always did. That’s how I knew there was a world beyond the Smoky Mountains.”</p>



<h2>How it works</h2>

<p><a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/the-dollywood-foundation/">Parton’s Dollywood Foundation covers</a> overhead and administrative expenses, coordinates the book selection committee, maintains the book order system and arranges orders and fulfillment.</p>

<p>The Imagination Library is available to any child in a community participating in the program, regardless of their family’s income.</p>

<p>To be eligible, a community must secure a local partner. Local partners publicize the program and enroll children. They have to pay US$2.60 per month per child to defray costs of purchasing books wholesale and mailing them. These partners include schools, public libraries and government agencies, and several kinds of nonprofits, including foundations.</p>

<p>Nonpartisan expert committees of educators and librarians select the books, nearly all <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/usa/book-list/">published by Penguin Random House</a>.</p>

<p>The program is continuing under the direction of the Dollywood Foundation’s president, Jeff Conyers. A <a href="https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/by-topic/childrens/childrens-industry-news/article/101140-dolly-parton-s-children-s-literacy-legacy.html">Penguin Random House vice president said</a>, “We
will continue that work with the utmost pride and care, just as we know she would have wanted.”</p>

<p>But <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/books/dolly-parton-imagination-library.html">funding challenges</a> have arisen in at least four states. </p>

<h2>Steady growth and diversification</h2>

<p>By 2001, the Imagination Library had expanded to affiliates in nearly a dozen states. The next year, it extended its reach to <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/news-resources/year-in-review/">92 Native American communities</a>, partnering with the Cherokee Nation, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Parents as Teachers and the National Center for Family Literacy.</p>

<p>In late 2003, the Imagination Library <a href="https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/print/20040105/20408-parton-s-library-hits-one-million.html">mailed its one-millionth book</a>. In 2004, it launched its first statewide program – fittingly, in Tennessee. </p>

<p>It added <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/news-resources/year-in-review/">bilingual titles in Spanish and English</a> in 2003 and launched a bilingual Spanish website in 2022. The Imagination Library also supplied audio and braille books for those who needed them beginning in 2011.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/ed/2018/03/01/589912466/dolly-parton-gives-the-gift-of-literacy-a-library-of-100-million-books">Parton celebrated</a> when the library mailed its 100-millionth book in 2018. “We never thought it would be this big,” she told NPR. “I just wanted to do something great for my dad and for my home county and, at the most, maybe a couple of counties over. But then it just took wings of its own.”</p>

<p>The Imagination Library shipped its 200-millionth book in 2023 and its 300-millionth book in 2025. By 2024, <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/about-us/">1 in 7 children under the age of 5 in the United States</a> were receiving books for free every month, courtesy of this initiative. </p>

<p>Other programs give free books to young children, including <a href="https://reachoutandread.org/">Reach Out and Read</a> in the U.S., which since 1989 has handed them out at children’s medical checkups. <a href="https://www.booktrust.org.uk/">Bookstart</a>, which launched in 1992, offers every baby in England, Wales and Northern Ireland a free book and tips on reading aloud to kids.</p>

<h2>Program benefits</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-016-0815-9">Parents and caregivers</a>
 <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">highly</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2023.2202179">praise</a> the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02568543.2024.2322731">program</a>.</p>

<p>Many studies have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00094056.2012.699850">children get excited about getting</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">their own books</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2023.2202179">in the mail</a>, addressed to them personally. Both they and their families also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00094056.2012.699850">take great pride in book</a> <a href="https://coloradolab.org/2025/08/13/evaluation-report-imagination-library-of-colorado/">ownership</a>.</p>

<p>“A lot of (children) wait at the mailbox at the first of the month,” Parton <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2000/03/23/the-reliable-source/9f3f768d-ea9f-4801-9252-45cb4e61ea5c/">told The Washington Post</a>. “They think that I bring the book myself, like I’m Santa Claus.”</p>

<p>As one parent <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">told an education researcher</a>, “We read the books when they come in the mail instead of watching TV.”</p>

<p>The library’s books “<a href="https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320922140">nudge</a>” children to make reading a regular habit. Many studies have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-016-0815-9">children who are read</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">to more frequently</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02568543.2024.2322731">by</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2023.2202179">their loved</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/09575146.2021.1908234">ones</a>, spend more time <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02568543.2024.2322731">reading together daily</a> and ask more frequently for books to be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">read to them</a>.</p>

<p>This program aims not only to boost a child’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-016-0815-9">love of reading</a> but to improve their cognitive development and get them ready for elementary school by enlarging their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">vocabulary and improving their listening skills</a>.</p>

<p>Kids who get the books tend to know more letters, understand how books and printed words work, recognize and retain words’ sounds, and both <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03004430.2026.2678212">understand and use more spoken words</a>. Similarly, <a href="https://coloradolab.org/2025/08/13/evaluation-report-imagination-library-of-colorado/">children enrolled in the program have scored higher</a> than their peers when they take a standard kindergarten entrance early-reading skills test.</p>

<p>In line with Parton’s original goal, the Imagination Library may do the most to change reading habits in <a href="https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320922140">lower-income homes</a> – where children’s books tend to be scarce.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292207/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Anthropic vs. the pope
excerpt: Anthropic’s Christopher Olah shakes hands with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on May 25, 2026. | Alberto Pizzoli / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in&nbsp
body: Anthropic’s Christopher Olah shakes hands with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on May 25, 2026. | Alberto Pizzoli / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Hi readers, happy Friday! It’s been a big week for the AI debate — not the one about whether it will cause the robot apocalypse, though there’s still plenty to worry about there, but instead about whether the technology is conscious.  The folks at Anthropic, the AI company behind the large language model Claude, certainly seem to think it is — or at least, they’re extremely open to the possibility.  As the New York Times reported earlier in the week, the company has spent the last year grappling with the question by speaking with religious thinkers from many faith traditions in an effort to chart a moral course for the LLM (that is, to keep it from killing us all, so maybe it is all one big debate).  In the process, the Times reports, some of those thinkers observed that members of the Anthropic team were “relating to [Claude] like a conscious being” and even, according to it, a degree of “moral status.”  On the flip side of this debate is Pope Leo XIV, who decidedly does not seem to buy into AI consciousness arguments
His “Magnifica Humanitas” encyclical earlier this year argued that AI will never be able to replace humanity — and reportedly “alarmed” Anthropic’s co-founder, Christopher Olah

Since then, Pope Leo has continued to emphasize the differences between humans and machines this week. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others,” he posted on Friday. “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.” Loneliness machines Conscious or no (and that’s a no from me), it’s hard to argue that tech companies don’t want you to interact with their models like people

That includes OpenAI and Meta, both of whom introduced “cute” new AI agents — called Dots and Muse, respectively — last month.  As my colleague Adam Clark Estes reported this week , though, the promise of a companionable, always-there AI might not be the best idea in the world — especially for children

A new study, still under review, suggests that AI use may be causing loneliness in middle schoolers.  Adam spoke with the lead researcher on the study, UNC Chapel Hill professor Anne Maheux, who  explained that “middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time.”  According to Maheux, one big point where AI chatbots fail compared to human beings is “friction,” or the complicated push-and-pull dynamic of any connection with a real human being

By contrast, chatbots are “sycophantic, highly agreeable, anthropomorphized,” she says, which can lead to kids “developing expectations or understandings of interactive relationships that are actually fundamentally at odds with a normal human relationship.” People, in other words, still matter, no matter how much the AI companies want us to build our lives around machines instead

title: The Cornell case, explained
